newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Firestorm erupts in Philippines over Ramos term.
newsitem.headline: Firestorm erupts in Philippines over Ramos term.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos faced a political firestorm on Monday after a senior aide revealed plans to amend the constitution so he could remain in power into the 21st century.

In a rare show of unity, opposition politicians, church representatives, leftist groups and businessmen attacked the move while former president Corazon Aquino, who in 1986 helped lead a popular revolt that ousted Ferdinand Marcos, vowed to lead street protests if needed.
The uproar helped depress the Manila stock market. The main index ended 0.22 percent down at 3,314.84 as some investors used the row as an excuse to stay on the sidelines or sell.
"I have stated categorically so many times before that I am against any amendments at this time because it will be so divisive," said Aquino.
"If it is necessary, then I will lead a march against amending the constitution," she told Reuters.

Ramos's Executive Secretary Ruben Torres stirred the uproar when he said at the weekend that many members of the Lakas (People Power) party favoured changing the constitution to allow Ramos to stay on for "at least" six more years.
Up until now, Ramos and his ministers have vigorously denied any plans to tinker with the constitution, which limits a president to only one term of six years.
Ramos, who will turn 69 next month, has repeatedly pledged to step down when his tenure ends in June 1998.

The ex-army general, whose reform programme has turned a once-lagging economy into one of the fastest-growing in Asia, told reporters Torres was merely thinking out loud. Lakas has not defined its position on the issue, he told reporters on Sunday.
Ramos, who has been touring the provinces since the row erupted, on Monday denounced opposition charges his aides were fomenting unrest to invite an army coup which he would lead.
Ramos accused his critics of "sowing intrigue and spreading wild and unfounded rumours," a palace statement said.
Business leaders voiced concern the political row might drive potential investors to adopt a wait-and-see attitude.

"That's not good for the economy," said Guillermo Luz, executive director of the prestigious Makati Business Club. "There's no question that President Ramos has done good for this country ... but the system is designed to accomodate change. The challenge is for us to pick a good leader (after Ramos).

"We want to get away from personality politics, we are for building democratic institutions," Luz added. "The fact that we can have growth in a democracy shows democracy works. Why tinker with a succesful model?"

"These talks about charter changes reduce predictability which is very crucial for investors. It adds confusion," said Cris Frianeze, secretary general of the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

Senator Edgardo Angara, the opposition chief and one of about a dozen politicians aspiring to succeed Ramos, called for nationwide protests "to crush this malevolent Lakas campaign". Leftist groups said they would also hold protest rallies.
Vice President Joseph Estrada, a former movie actor regarded by many as the man to beat in next year's polls, said on Sunday he would launch a campaign to thwart any move to change the charter.

Monsignor Pedro Quitorio, spokesman of the influental Roman Catholic Church, said the country's bishops also opposed amending the constitution and would issue a statement shortly spelling out their position.
Other opposition senators warned of what they called a "creeping dictatorship".
